paragraphs.en: Acute ischemic stroke (AIS), accounting for approximately 80% of all stroke cases, represents a critical challenge to global health as a leading cause of mortality, disability, and economic burden worldwide [1]. This condition, caused by an abrupt cessation of blood flow to the brain, demands immediate medical intervention due to its rapid and devastating impact on neuronal health. Within just five minutes of ischemia, brain cells begin to perish, with estimates suggesting that each minute of delayed treatment results in the loss of approximately 1.9 million neurons and 14 billion synapses [2]. Accurate and timely diagnosis is therefore vital for administering thrombolysis and thrombectomy, the two main treatment strategies for AIS, both of which are highly time-sensitive and depend on precise imaging-based decision-making [3]. Such statistics [4–6] underscore the critical importance of timely and accurate diagnosis, as well as swift decision-making, in mitigating the catastrophic effects of AIS.

The management and treatment of AIS require not only rapid diagnostics but also specialised expertise and long-term monitoring. Given the challenges posed by geographically dispersed medical institutions, disparities in healthcare quality, and the diverse characteristics of AIS patients, a collaborative approach is indispensable. In this regard, Collaborative Artificial Intelligence (CAI) [7] plays a pivotal role by providing a secure, efficient, and equitable framework for knowledge and model sharing among institutions. Traditionally, CAI refers to AI systems involving direct collaboration with experts who possess domain knowledge and practical experience. In this paper, however, we extend the concept by integrating it with federated learning(FL) [8,9] and distributed artificial intelligence [10], viewing models as the cognitive processing and refinement of data performed by such experts. Based on this perspective, collaboration among models represents an intelligent form of inter-institutional cooperation, enabling models themselves to act as agents of knowledge exchange and joint reasoning. Unlike conventional single-centre AI systems that often suffer from data scarcity or institutional bias, CAI enables multi-institutional collaboration without compromising patient privacy, allowing models to learn from a broader and more diverse patient population. The CAI refers to a decentralised framework where models, rather than raw data, are shared and jointly optimised across multiple institutions through mechanisms such as federated learning and privacy-preserving computation [11–13]. By leveraging advanced technologies, the CAI can assist less-equipped institutions in delivering better care. Through secure information sharing and aggregation, AI models can be trained on diverse datasets from multiple institutions, enhancing their precision and generalisation capabilities. This approach not only bridges gaps in healthcare expertise but also fosters a more equitable and effective framework for AIS management, ultimately improving patient outcomes [14–18].

The implementation of CAI in AIS diagnosis and management is critically challenged by data privacy concerns, especially in sensitive medical environments where patient information must remain confidential. Regulatory frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) [19] in the European Union and the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) [20] in the United States impose stringent requirements on data collection, storage, and sharing, complicating efforts to implement AI solutions across institutions. While data-sharing mechanisms are widely applicable across various medical domains, AIS presents distinctive challenges due to its time-critical nature, imaging heterogeneity, and multimodal diagnostic characteristics. Effective diagnosis requires rapid integration of information from diverse imaging modalities (e.g. CT, MRI, angiography) and coordination among geographically dispersed medical centres. Moreover, ensuring equitable access to advanced diagnostic resources and addressing disparities in healthcare quality further amplify the necessity for a collaborative and privacy-preserving AI framework. In this context, CAI emerges as a promising approach to address these challenges. By enabling collaborative model training without requiring data to leave its source, it ensures the security and privacy of sensitive information while leveraging diverse datasets to improve AI model accuracy and generalization. This is particularly valuable in AIS diagnosis, where timely and precise medical decisions are critical. A collaborative framework integrating medical expertise and AI not only ensures equitable access to advanced diagnostic tools but also strengthens healthcare systems by enhancing diagnostic accuracy, accelerating treatment decisions, and bridging resource gaps across institutions. Such a framework holds significant research value by addressing disparities in healthcare quality, enabling data-driven decision-making, and fostering innovation in medical collaboration. Moreover, it paves the way for more robust, scalable, and adaptable solutions, ultimately improving patient outcomes and advancing the field of precision medicine.

Currently, numerous review articles have thoughtfully summarized and meticulously analysed these advancements [14,15,18,21–30]. These comprehensive reviews offer valuable insights into the ever-evolving landscape of stroke management. They accentuate the pivotal role played by AI and machine learning in enhancing diagnostic precision, optimising treatment decisions, and ultimately enhancing patient outcomes. To the best of our knowledge, this paper is the first to explore the integration of CAI with AIS from the perspective of real-world multi-institutional collaboration. The framework of this review is shown in Figure 1. We present a perspective-style review that explores how CAI may reshape the diagnosis and management of AIS. Unlike previous reviews limited to AI applications in AIS, we highlight the critical importance of developing collaborative frameworks that address the real-world needs and operational diversity of healthcare institutions. We also provide a comprehensive analysis of the technologies, feasibility, and recommendations for implementing CAI in AIS diagnosis and treatment. To ensure balanced and comprehensive coverage, we conducted a staged, coarse-to-fine literature search to identify influential and emerging studies. We first surveyed a broad range of related works and then refined the scope to those of clear clinical or methodological relevance. Considering that some frontier studies have not yet been formally published, we also included grey literature to capture the latest advances. These sources collectively provided a robust foundation for mapping current trends and identifying research gaps in CAI for AIS. By examining emerging challenges and proposing solutions through intelligent and privacy-enhancing technologies, we not only survey current AI applications but also detail CAI-compatible platforms and offer tailored guidance for varying institutional needs. Furthermore, we identify key future directions for advancing CAI innovations in AIS, bridging the gap between technical development and practical deployment.

AI has made substantial contributions to both the diagnosis and tailored treatment of AIS. Machine learning techniques have found extensive applications in this domain, spanning various critical aspects. It’s important to note that the relevant work discussed here primarily focuses on the latest research conducted within the past three years. These encompass the early identification of diagnostic imaging markers [31,32], precise estimation of stroke onset time [33,34], meticulous lesion segmentation [35,36], determination of tissue viability in at-risk regions [37,38], thorough analysis of cerebral edema [39,40], the proactive forecasting of potential complications [41,42] and patient outcomes following treatment interventions [43,44]. It should be emphasized that most of these AI-driven studies currently serve as research references or decision-support prototypes rather than established standards in clinical practice. Their primary value lies in risk warning, auxiliary decision-making, and the early exploration of personalized treatment potential. These significant strides in AI-driven healthcare underscore a deepening comprehension of the intricate nature of this condition, fostering the prospect of more individualized and efficacious treatment regimens.

The process of early detection of diagnostic imaging markers, critical in modern medicine, relies heavily on advanced technologies like Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) or Computed Tomography (CT) scans. These technologies detect subtle yet crucial changes that indicate disease onset, including organ morphological alterations and tissue structural abnormalities. Integrating AI with these imaging methods not only improves the speed and accuracy of diagnoses but also potentially transforms disease understanding and treatment by uncovering new characteristics. At this stage, AI-assisted imaging analysis primarily serves as a decision-support tool rather than a definitive clinical diagnostic standard, offering supplementary insights to clinicians for early risk identification and treatment planning. This AI integration represents a significant advancement in medical diagnostics and treatment strategies. Chiang et al. [31] introduced a groundbreaking deep learning-based automatic detection (DLAD) algorithm for automating Alberta Stroke Program Early CT Score (ASPECTS) evaluation in AIS using non-contrast CT (NCCT) scans. Involving 258 patient images, the study demonstrated DLAD’s notable performance with 65% sensitivity, 82% specificity and 80% accuracy. This work highlights the potential of AI to enhance the efficiency of AIS diagnosis. Verclytte et al. [32] introduced an AI-enhanced MRI protocol designed for rapid AIS diagnosis, completing scans in under 2 min using advanced Echo Planar Imaging techniques for various sequences. Tested on 173 patients with 80 confirmed cases of AIS, the protocol demonstrated strong agreement with traditional MRI methods in detecting AIS lesions and assessing vascular and parenchymal changes. The findings suggest that this AI-driven approach can significantly speed up the AIS diagnostic process.

Accurately estimating the onset time of a stroke is essential for acute management, as therapeutic options are strictly time-sensitive. Recent AI-driven studies have shown great potential in narrowing this critical window by integrating clinical and imaging data to support faster and more precise decision-making. Rather than replacing conventional assessment, these approaches complement clinicians’ expertise by providing quantitative evidence and probabilistic judgments that enhance confidence in time-related evaluations. Yang et al. [33] presented a novel classification model utilizing Computed Tomography Perfusion (CTP) to accurately classify the time since stroke onset (TSS) in AIS patients, employing dynamic convolution, multi-scale feature fusion, and multi-head pooling attention to enhance model representation and achieve at least 5% higher accuracy in TSS classification compared to existing methods. Zhang et al. [34] developed deep learning models that employ MRI diffusion series with a novel intra-domain task-adaptive transfer learning strategy to enhance TSS classification in AIS patients. Demonstrating improved accuracy, this approach shows considerable promise for treating patients with indeterminate TSS and underscores the potential of sophisticated computational models to refine clinical decision-making in AIS management.

Integrating AI with meticulous lesion segmentation presents a significant advancement in medical imaging, offering enhanced diagnostic accuracy and treatment planning. This AI-enabled approach automates the precise delineation of pathological areas in imaging studies, such as MRI or CT scans, reducing human error and variability. Although these techniques are not yet established as clinical diagnostic standards, they have demonstrated substantial potential as assistive tools for improving lesion characterisation, guiding therapeutic decisions, and supporting personalised treatment planning. The clinical implications are notable, improving lesion detection and supporting personalised treatment strategies. Such integration marks a crucial step forward in personalised medicine, optimising therapeutic interventions and elevating patient care standards. Lee et al. [35] demonstrated that convolutional neural networks(CNNs), specifically Inception-v3 and a modified LeNet, can effectively detect ischemic strokes and classify them by circulation area using early-stage Diffusion-Weighted Imaging (DWI). Their findings underscore the benefits of transfer learning in enhancing stroke imaging and patient outcomes. Liu et al. [36] developed an ensemble of deep learning networks for detecting and segmenting ischemic stroke lesions in MRI scans, achieving high accuracy on a substantial clinical dataset. Their model excels in identifying small lesions and is both robust and generalizable, making it publicly accessible for swift and straightforward use.

Salvageable Tissue Identification in AIS is crucial for highlighting brain regions at risk yet viable for recovery with prompt intervention. Effective identification of these areas is essential for enhancing patient recovery and reducing long-term neurological damage. Although current AI-based techniques remain primarily at the research stage, they have shown substantial promise as supportive tools for clinicians, offering quantitative evidence to assist in assessing tissue viability and guiding reperfusion decisions. Vupputuri et al. [38] developed a multi-view iterative random walker algorithm, an automated method for segmenting and quantifying ischemic tissues in stroke lesions via multi-view MRI analyses. This approach improves lesion classification and enhances treatment planning, potentially boosting patient survival outcomes. Vupputuri et al. [37] developed MCA-DN, a novel model combining multi-path convolution with attention mechanisms, significantly enhancing MRI-based stroke lesion segmentation. It efficiently segments and analyses the ischemic penumbra and necrotic core using multi-sequence MRI, improving the accuracy of identifying salvageable tissue in stroke-affected areas.

Cerebral edema involves the problematic buildup of fluid in the brain, posing diagnostic and treatment challenges. Traditional diagnostic methods, reliant on the subjective interpretation of medical imaging, often lack consistency and speed. The integration of AI into this process revolutionizes the analysis, providing precision and accelerating diagnosis. Bui et al. [39] proposed an automated image analysis pipeline to quantify cerebral edema in stroke patients through cerebrospinal fluid displacement and ratio metrics, demonstrating that these volumetric biomarkers can effectively measure edema severity beyond traditional methods, are influenced by stroke severity and vascular risk factors, and are associated with worse stroke outcomes. Foroushani et al. [40] introduced a long short-term memory (LSTM) neural network, utilizing volumetric data from routine CT scans, significantly outperformed traditional regression models. This approach demonstrates potential in enabling timely surgical interventions and underscores the effectiveness of imaging-based machine learning models in identifying suitable candidates for decompressive hemicraniectomy. These AI-based methods are currently at the experimental and validation stages, yet they show strong potential as adjunctive tools that assist clinicians in quantifying edema progression, guiding surgical considerations, and optimizing patient monitoring strategies.

The use of AI for predicting hemorrhagic transformation (HT) in ischemic stroke patients provides a promising avenue for improving individualised risk assessment, although current approaches remain largely investigational. Advanced AI algorithms analyse clinical data and imaging biomarkers to assist clinicians in identifying patients at higher risk of post-treatment hemorrhage, which is particularly relevant when evaluating eligibility for thrombolysis or thrombectomy. These models thus function as decision-support systems that can enhance safety in acute management, even though they have not yet been formally adopted in clinical guidelines. Meng et al. [42] developed a predictive model for HT in AIS patients using 5,400 radiomic features from multiparametric MRI combined with clinical factors, demonstrating that incorporating both normal and abnormal tissue regions improved prediction accuracy. Similarly, Elsaid et al. [41] identified cerebral microbleeds, National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score, and infarction size as significant predictors of HT, with random forest and gradient boosting methods outperforming linear classifiers. While these studies highlight important nonlinear interactions between imaging and clinical features, further multi-centre validation and real-world trials are required before routine clinical integration.

AI significantly enhances treatment outcome analysis for critical conditions, offering advanced analytics for a detailed understanding of therapeutic effects. This technology enables precise evaluations and improves clinical decision-making by predicting patient responses and identifying potential side effects. Lai et al. [44] leveraged a VGG-16 network, trained with MRI data from ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke patients, to accurately predict 28-day functional outcomes, demonstrating the model’s high accuracy and offering an automated decision support system for personalised stroke patient care. Hatami et al. [43] introduced a novel multi-modal CNN-LSTM-based ensemble model that integrates heterogeneous data for stroke outcome prediction, combining MR image analysis with clinical metadata like age or NIHSS, achieving the highest AUC of 0.77 and offering a pioneering deep learning solution to support clinical decision-making in acute stroke management.

In the AI-enabled applications of AIS, transitioning from theory to practice reveals numerous obstacles. Core challenges include limited data access, uneven medical technology distribution, and the essential need for trust in AI systems. Particularly, stringent data privacy laws and the lack of annotated medical datasets restrict AI’s potential, leading to isolated data silos and underutilization of data. Moreover, the uneven allocation of technological resources exacerbates regional disparities, impacting the equitable deployment of AI and the creation of diverse training datasets. Trustworthy CAI deployment in healthcare demands a balance between privacy, fairness, and model explainability.

Federated Learning(FL) emerges as a robust solution to these complex challenges. By enabling collaborative model training across diverse institutions while eliminating the need for direct data sharing, FL effectively addresses privacy concerns inherent in traditional methods. This approach not only expands the range of data available for CAI innovations but also ensures compliance with privacy regulations. FL democratizes participation in CAI model training, addressing fairness by utilising diverse datasets to mitigate bias and promote equitable medical solutions. Furthermore, the collaborative nature of FL training improves the interpretability and transparency of AI models, essential for building trust among clinicians and patients. Incorporating privacy, fairness, and explainability into the CAI development process via trustworthy FL not only sidesteps the practical barriers to data sharing but also adheres to the ethical standards of healthcare. Thus, trustworthy FL emerges as a crucial technological strategy in advancing AI research and its application in AIS management, setting a foundation for ethical, equitable, and efficacious healthcare solutions within the computational domain, signifying a major stride towards realising the full potential of CAI in enhancing patient care and treatment outcomes.

The concept of FL was initially proposed by Google [8,9,45], originally aimed at addressing the issue of updating models on Android devices locally. The core idea revolves around constructing machine learning models based on datasets distributed across multiple devices while preventing data leakage. The framework of FL is demonstrated in Figure 2. Recent works in this domain have primarily focused on overcoming statistical challenges [46–48], enhancing the security of FL [9,49,50], and striving to make FL more personalised [46,51,52]. These research efforts concentrate on FL across devices, users, and institutions, involving key optimisation factors such as user interactions across multiple devices, communication costs in large-scale distribution, imbalanced data distributions, and cross-institutional reliability [9]. Additionally, with the growing concerns of algorithmic bias and the advancement in algorithmic fairness research [53–57], some studies such as [58–61] have gradually begun to address performance fairness issues arising from resource disparities among participants in FL. These works have demonstrated the powerful capabilities and potential of FL in artificial intelligence medical applications.

Essentially, the majority of AI work enabling AIS can be adapted and optimised for a federated setting to address the aforementioned challenges and issues. In the following section, we introduce trustworthy FL for AIS. Given the relatively few direct applications of FL in AIS, we review the application of FL in other diseases and healthcare-related tasks. By analysing the similarities in scenarios between these applications and AIS, we aim to illustrate the potential and capabilities of FL in AIS.

In [62], FL was applied to train deep learning models across different medical centers without sharing patient data, using novel weighting functions to successfully address dataset imbalance and data heterogeneity, significantly improving segmentation tasks for stroke and brain tumour on multi-centric datasets. Madrona et al. [63] utilized FL with the FedAvg algorithm in a multi-centre scenario involving 286 acute stroke patients, demonstrating its effectiveness in maintaining segmentation performance despite data heterogeneity and limited data sharing, presenting a feasible alternative for stroke segmentation in diverse clinical settings. Victor et al. [64] proposed a privacy-preserving machine learning framework for early brain stroke prediction using FL, optimized with Particle Swarm Optimization for enhanced accuracy, which outperformed other models in experimental evaluations.

Beyond algorithmic fairness and privacy-preserving mechanisms, real-world deployment of medical AI must also meet stringent regulatory and ethical standards. Global frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) in the European Union, the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) in the United States, and Japan’s Act on the Protection of Personal Information (APPI) have underscored transparency, interpretability, and user consent in medical data use. These principles place strong constraints on non-collaborative AI systems, where centralised data collection often violates data localisation and cross-border transfer regulations, as shown in Table 1.

Globally, data protection regulations such as the GDPR, CCPA, APPI, PIPL and PDPA establish stringent requirements for transparency, user consent, data minimisation, and localisation in healthcare AI. In non-collaborative AI systems, compliance typically requires centralised data aggregation, explicit cross-border consent, and rigorous auditing of model provenance. These processes are often costly, time-consuming, and susceptible to privacy risks. Moreover, such systems frequently encounter regulatory challenges under data localisation laws and may struggle to ensure fairness across underrepresented populations due to limited data diversity. In contrast, CAI adopts privacy-preserving mechanisms such as federated learning, secure aggregation, and differential privacy, allowing models to learn from distributed data sources without exposing sensitive patient information. This decentralised paradigm naturally aligns with international regulatory expectations, enabling compliant, auditable, and ethically responsible cross-institutional collaboration. In addition, for non-collaborative AI tools that rely on centralised data or closed-source algorithms, developers and institutions should establish clear data usage agreements, conduct bias and safety audits prior to clinical deployment, and ensure continuous monitoring for model drift or unintended harm. Independent third-party validation and transparency reporting are also recommended to maintain regulatory trust and patient safety. However, a detailed discussion of compliance strategies for non-collaborative AI systems is beyond the scope of this paper and will not be elaborated further here.

In the field of AIS, implementing and applying practical measures of FL involves establishing an efficient cross-institutional collaboration platform to drive the development of disease diagnosis and treatment methods. Leveraging existing FL technology and incorporating the needs of domain experts, this platform ensures knowledge sharing and model collaboration while ensuring data security and privacy protection. Initially, each participating institution establishes a secure and reliable data channel with a third-party FL platform, facilitating collaboration in data sharing and model training. Subsequently, the platform offers unified model management and services, enabling institutions to upload their models or choose from a provided model repository tailored for tasks such as ischemic stroke image recognition and clinical prediction, either as pre-trained models or optimised models under the FL framework.

In terms of data management, the platform adopts FL, allowing each participating institution to retain and manage its data locally, ensuring data remains within the original institutions. Data processing and computation occur locally, with model parameters and update information transmitted securely to the platform for model aggregation and optimisation, ensuring data privacy. Moreover, the platform provides a rich algorithm library and computational resources to support model training and optimisation under the FL environment, dynamically allocating resources based on task requirements to balance computational efficiency and model performance. The platform operates with high automation and scalability, facilitating close collaboration and data sharing among institutions through advanced technological means, thereby providing robust support for AIS diagnosis and treatment. Additionally, the platform’s establishment lays the groundwork for future collaborative research and cooperation in broader medical domains.

To reinforce trustworthiness, it is imperative to utilise privacy protection technologies to prioritise the security of local data and models. This ensures that sensitive patient information remains confidential and inaccessible to unauthorised parties throughout the FL process. To address the privacy challenges arising from knowledge sharing among different parties, various privacy-preserving techniques have been proposed, including Differential Privacy (DP) [11,87], Homomorphic Encryption (HE) [12,88], Secure Multi-Party Computation (MPC) [13,89], and hybrid methods [90,91]. DP provides a strong privacy guarantee by adding noise to the output of a computation, making it difficult for attackers to extract sensitive information from the result. HE allows computation on encrypted data without decrypting it, which can prevent unauthorised access to sensitive data. MPC enables multiple parties to jointly compute a function while keeping their inputs private, but it can be computationally expensive and communication-intensive. Hybrid methods combine the benefits of multiple privacy-preserving techniques and can achieve better performance than individual methods alone. These mechanisms allow computations to be performed on protected local data without compromising its privacy, thereby safeguarding sensitive information while enabling collaborative model training.

In collaborative AI applications for AIS diagnosis and treatment, several privacy risks arise due to the involvement of sensitive medical data from multiple institutions. A major concern is data leakage, where patient data might be unintentionally exposed during model training or while aggregating updates from different sources. Another significant risk is inference attacks, such as model inversion or membership inference, where adversaries may attempt to deduce private information about individual patients from the shared model updates. Additionally, there is the threat of model poisoning, where malicious actors could intentionally inject harmful data into the collaborative process, skewing the model’s predictions. Ensuring compliance with healthcare regulations like GDPR and CCPA is also a challenge, as institutions must safeguard sensitive patient data while collaborating across different regions.

FL offers several strategies to mitigate these privacy risks effectively. By allowing data to remain local at each institution, FL minimises the risk of data leakage, as only model updates are shared, not the actual patient data. Techniques such as DP add noise to the model updates, making it difficult for adversaries to infer individual patient information, thereby protecting against inference attacks. HE ensures that model updates remain encrypted during transmission and aggregation, preventing the exposure of sensitive data. Furthermore, secure aggregation protocols prevent the reconstruction of individual data from the aggregated model updates, even if one institution’s update is compromised. These privacy-enhancing features ensure that FL-based solutions can maintain strict compliance with privacy regulations while still enabling effective collaboration in AIS diagnosis and treatment.

Currently, numerous federated platforms are integrating various types of FL algorithms [92]. proposes an open-source federated platform called FedEYE, focusing specifically on ophthalmic diseases. This platform shares significant commonality and relevance with applications for AIS and demonstrates potential for practical deployment. By integrating multiple FL algorithms, FedEYE provides a feasible solution for data sharing and model training in the ophthalmic domain. FATE (Federated AI Technology Enabler) [93] is an open-source project initiated by Webank’s AI Department to provide a secure computing framework supporting the federated AI ecosystem. It implements multiple secure computation protocols, including HE and MPC, enabling enterprises and institutions to collaborate on data while protecting data security and privacy. FedML [94] is designed to facilitate FL by providing a unified and scalable machine learning library. It supports large-scale distributed training, model serving, and federated learning across various devices and environments, including decentralised GPUs, multi-clouds, edge servers, and smartphones. FederatedScope [95] is a comprehensive FL platform designed to provide users with flexible and easy-to-use tools for various FL tasks in both academic and industrial settings. It employs an event-driven architecture, allowing users to independently define the behaviours of different participants, which facilitates the handling of heterogeneity in data, resources, and learning objectives. PySyft [96], TensorFlow Federated [97], and PaddleFL [98] are also prominent open-source frameworks designed to facilitate federated learning, enabling collaborative model training across decentralised data sources while preserving data privacy. These frameworks are instrumental in advancing privacy-preserving machine learning by enabling collaborative model training across diverse and distributed datasets.

FedEYE exhibits unique advantages when applied to ophthalmic diseases and has undergone thorough comparisons and validations in both experimental and real-world scenarios. FedEYE not only offers a rich array of FL algorithms but also customizes optimizations to meet the specific needs and characteristics of ophthalmic diseases. This customization allows the platform to better adapt to the unique data characteristics and medical tasks associated with AIS, improving model accuracy and generalization. For instance, in collaborative AIS diagnosis, customization is essential to accommodate the heterogeneous nature of patient populations, such as differences in age, gender, and comorbidities across institutions. Additionally, the platform can be tailored to handle the unique characteristics of brain imaging data, such as CT and MRI scans, and specific diagnostic tasks like detecting vessel blockages or predicting patient outcomes. Effective integration of multimodal data is also crucial. Furthermore, optimizing FL for specific objectives—such as balancing diagnostic accuracy with real-time processing in emergency settings—requires customization to meet the distinct needs of each participating institution. FedEYE also considers the importance of data privacy and security, employing advanced privacy protection techniques to ensure the safety and confidentiality of patient data. Thus, the platform not only excels in technical performance but also demonstrates high credibility and reliability in data security and privacy protection. Therefore, the federated platform FedEYE, focusing on ophthalmic diseases, introduces new perspectives and methodologies for FL applications in medical fields like AIS. It showcases significant potential and practical application prospects in the healthcare domain and serves as a reference for future related applications.

The market features a wide array of large-scale commercial FL platforms, including NVIDIA Clara1, Microsoft Azure2, and IBM Watson3, and others. Compared to open-source platforms, these commercial platforms often come with significant drawbacks. Firstly, they can be costly, requiring subscription fees or other charges that may be prohibitive for smaller organisations. Secondly, they generally demand higher hardware specifications and computing resources, which can lead to additional investments in infrastructure. Thirdly, these platforms typically have a steeper learning curve, requiring more specialised knowledge or training to use effectively. Additionally, commercial solutions might offer less flexibility for customisation as they are usually designed to serve a broad range of needs, which may not align perfectly with specific organisational requirements.

Selecting an appropriate FL platform is contingent upon several factors, such as the institution’s specific needs, the nature of the tasks, and the operational context. For example, several hospitals across different regions are collaborating to improve AIS diagnosis using brain imaging data. By using FL platforms, each hospital trains a local model on its data and shares only model updates, ensuring patient privacy while enhancing diagnostic accuracy. This collaboration results in a more accurate AI model for AIS diagnosis, leveraging diverse datasets to improve early detection and treatment outcomes, while also balancing healthcare resources and enabling remote, underserved areas to benefit from expert-level diagnostic services.

In this context, FedEYE emerges as a highly adaptable and promising FL platform, particularly for AIS diagnosis and treatment. Although originally optimised for ophthalmic diseases, FedEYE’s features make it well-suited for AIS applications. Below, we provide a detailed analysis of how FedEYE can be leveraged for AIS, emphasising its key strengths and comparing it with other FL platforms to assess its applicability in this domain.

A core advantage of FedEYE is its robust privacy-preserving mechanism. FL enables decentralized data processing, meaning that sensitive AIS data, such as brain imaging scans, remains securely stored at the originating institution, rather than being shared across a centralized server. This is essential in AIS, where patient confidentiality and regulatory compliance are critical. FedEYE further enhances privacy through techniques like DP and HE, making it an ideal platform for AIS, where data security is paramount.

AIS diagnosis requires collaboration between multiple medical institutions, which may have access to different types of medical imaging data, including CT and MRI scans of the brain. FedEYE facilitates collaborative research by enabling institutions to train machine learning models collaboratively without sharing sensitive data. This is particularly beneficial in AIS, where aggregating data from multiple institutions can improve diagnostic accuracy. By leveraging this feature, FedEYE allows for the pooling of expertise and data to develop more reliable diagnostic models, improving both early detection and treatment outcomes.

The ability to scale and deploy efficiently is a critical factor when selecting an FL platform for AIS. FedEYE supports flexible deployment across cloud and edge computing environments, which is crucial for AIS, where real-time analysis of medical images may be required during acute phases. The platform supports a wide range of hardware configurations, from CPUs and GPUs to specialised FPGAs, ensuring that it can be integrated seamlessly into existing healthcare infrastructures. The edge-cloud collaboration enabled by FedEYE allows for faster model inference at the point of care, providing timely decision support in AIS emergencies.

FedEYE is designed with a low-code interface, making it accessible to medical professionals without deep programming expertise. This feature is crucial for AIS, as clinicians and researchers can focus on diagnostic tasks rather than managing complex coding or machine learning processes. The intuitive, user-friendly interface allows medical staff to configure and initiate FL tasks with ease, facilitating the adoption of AI-driven tools in AIS diagnosis. This lowers the barrier to entry for healthcare institutions, promoting broader collaboration and the use of AI in clinical workflows.

sections.title: Data pool, task pool, and algorithm pool

paragraphs.en: FedEYE’s architecture includes several essential components that enhance its operational efficiency and flexibility:(1) Data Pool. The Data Pool stores and manages the datasets required for FL tasks. It ensures that data is appropriately partitioned and distributed across the participating institutions, which is essential for AIS applications where large datasets from various hospitals need to be aggregated while ensuring privacy. (2) Task Pool. The Task Pool allows users to define, manage, and monitor different FL tasks. For AIS, this can include tasks like training models for brain imaging classification or AIS outcome prediction. By organising these tasks into a pool, the platform facilitates efficient task management, making it easier to scale and prioritise critical tasks in real-time clinical environments. (3) Algorithm Pool. The Algorithm Pool contains a variety of machine learning models and algorithms that are optimised for different types of data and tasks. For AIS, models trained for image analysis (e.g. CT scans, and MRI scans) can be selected from this pool and fine-tuned for specific diagnostic purposes. The platform also supports algorithm aggregation, allowing the best-performing models to be combined to improve accuracy.

FedEYE offers several advantages over other FL platforms such as FATE, FedML, and PySyft, particularly in the context of AIS diagnosis. Unlike general-purpose FL frameworks like FATE and PySyft, which are not optimized for specific domains, FedEYE is specifically tailored for medical applications. Its optimization for handling medical image data, such as fundus images, allows it to be easily adapted to AIS-related imaging tasks like brain CT and MRI scans. Additionally, FedEYE’s modular architecture facilitates seamless integration with existing medical systems, a feature that is often lacking in other platforms that may require significant customization for AIS-specific needs. Moreover, FedEYE supports both horizontal and vertical FL, enabling it to scale efficiently and handle large datasets from multiple institutions, whether the data is distributed independently (IID) or not (non-IID). This flexibility is particularly valuable in AIS, where data from diverse hospitals and imaging centres need to be aggregated and processed collaboratively. These combined features make FedEYE a highly effective and adaptable platform for AIS diagnosis.

sections.title: Institutional collaboration and customization in FL for AIS

paragraphs.en: Different healthcare institutions, such as academic centres and local hospitals, can leverage FL platforms for AIS diagnosis, but their specific needs and challenges differ based on factors like institutional size, data availability, and resources. Academic centres, with their larger datasets, advanced computational resources, and specialized research teams, are well-equipped to contribute significant expertise to the FL systems. They can focus on developing cutting-edge models and conducting complex analyses using diverse AIS data from a wide range of patient demographics. However, they may face challenges in managing large-scale data and ensuring that models are applicable across different healthcare settings.

In contrast, local hospitals typically have smaller datasets and fewer computational resources, but they often deal with high-throughput, real-time cases in emergency settings. For these institutions, FL platforms offer a valuable opportunity to collaborate with larger centres, benefiting from advanced models developed by academic institutions while also contributing their own real-time patient data. This collaboration allows local hospitals to access the expertise and resources of larger institutions without the need for extensive in-house computational capabilities. However, challenges for local hospitals include ensuring data privacy, meeting regulatory requirements, and adapting models to their local patient populations, which may differ in terms of demographics and healthcare needs.

To address these challenges, FL platforms should be customised to fit the specific resources and needs of each institution. For example, smaller hospitals might require more lightweight models that can run on local devices with limited computational capacity, while larger centres may need more complex models capable of handling a wide variety of data inputs. Moreover, FL platforms provide low-barrier access to high-quality medical expertise from anywhere, enabling institutions with limited resources to benefit from the knowledge and models developed by leading experts. Additionally, the platform should include flexible data-sharing and aggregation mechanisms, ensuring that all institutions, regardless of size, can participate in the collaborative learning process while maintaining patient privacy and data security. This creates a dynamic environment where all healthcare institutions, from local hospitals to academic centres, can collectively enhance AIS diagnosis and treatment without compromising the quality of care. This section briefly outlines the application of FL in AIS and compares mainstream collaborative platforms, providing valuable references for researchers and contributing to the advancement of privacy-preserving, data-sharing techniques in AIS diagnosis and treatment.

sections.title: Practical evidence and ongoing trials of FL in AIS

paragraphs.en: FL has already achieved notable success across various medical domains, demonstrating its ability to leverage heterogeneous, multi-modal data such as imaging, electronic health records (EHRs), physiological signals, and genomics for collaborative model development without compromising patient privacy. Applications in oncology, ophthalmology, and radiology have shown that FL can effectively integrate multi-institutional data, enhance model generalisation, and accelerate real-world translation. These proven advantages suggest that FL frameworks are also highly adaptable to the context of AIS, where timely diagnosis, multi-modal imaging interpretation, and risk prediction are critical yet often hindered by fragmented data ownership and strict privacy regulations.

Currently, several pioneering studies have explored the application of FL in AIS-related tasks. For example, Rangel et al. [99] developed a 14-centre federated framework for DWI/Apparent Diffusion Coefficient (ADC) infarct segmentation and reported a mean Dice coefficient of 0.71±0.24, maintaining 0.64±0.29 on out-of-distribution centres without retraining, demonstrating superior cross-site robustness compared to centralised and other aggregation strategies. Roca et al. [100] extended this concept to BrainAGE estimation in post-stroke patients, where a 16-centre FL model outperformed single-site baselines and achieved near-centralised performance, underscoring the feasibility of privacy-preserving biomarker modelling in multi-centre cohorts. Kim et al. [101] further compared in-silo FL and centralised learning for infarct and white matter lesion segmentation, finding that FL maintained comparable Dice scores while effectively mitigating domain-shift across institutions. Beyond imaging, Ju et al. [102] implemented FL for stroke risk prediction using distributed EHRs, achieving 10% to 20% higher predictive accuracy than models trained locally at individual hospitals. In parallel, Protani et al. [103] utilised federated Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to assess stroke severity based on EEG data, obtaining an MAE of 3.23 for NIHSS prediction—approaching expert-level accuracy. In real-time applications, Elhanashi et al. [104] integrated FL with YOLOv8 to detect facial paralysis symptoms for early stroke screening, maintaining competitive performance under privacy-preserving, latency-constrained environments. Collectively, these studies indicate that FL offers consistent benefits in AIS scenarios, including improved model generalisation, enhanced robustness in low-resource institutions, and strong privacy compliance. While most current evidence is derived from experimental or prototype systems, the upward trend in both performance and scalability suggests that federated and collaborative AI frameworks are on the verge of translating from research prototypes to clinically validated systems for stroke diagnosis and management.

sections.title: Fairness and subgroup generalization in CAI

paragraphs.en: A critical concern for deploying artificial intelligence in clinical practice is whether models maintain consistent performance across diverse patient subgroups. Variations in age, sex, ethnicity, and comorbidities often lead to biases in model performance, particularly when training data are collected from limited or homogeneous sources. CAI, when implemented through FL, offers a structural solution to this problem by enabling multi-institutional training while preserving local data privacy. Through decentralized collaboration, models can leverage demographically and geographically diverse datasets, thereby improving generalization and mitigating overfitting to dominant cohorts. Recent studies have demonstrated that fairness-aware federated approaches can effectively reduce subgroup disparities. Methods such as contribution-weighted aggregation, group-normalized optimization, and fairness-aware client selection have shown measurable improvements in balancing performance among participating institutions. For instance, benchmarking efforts in medical imaging [56,105] reported up to a 20% reduction in subgroup AUC variance when employing adaptive aggregation and normalization techniques compared to vanilla FedAvg, indicating enhanced equity in predictive outcomes across subpopulations. Similarly, collaborative fairness formulations [83] and fairness-aware selection algorithms [115] highlight that institutional heterogeneity—once a limitation—can be harnessed to improve fairness and reliability.

Nevertheless, while CAI inherently promotes inclusiveness through data diversity, structural fairness alone is insufficient. Ongoing research should incorporate explicit subgroup fairness metrics—such as demographic parity, equal opportunity, and subgroup-wise calibration—and establish continuous auditing pipelines for bias detection during model deployment. These strategies will be crucial for ensuring that CAI frameworks not only generalise across populations but also deliver trustworthy and equitable diagnostic support in real-world clinical environments.

sections.title: Future perspectives on trustworthy CAI for AIS

paragraphs.en: To improve the rapid service response time caused by the specific nature of AIS, future CAI applications can focus on optimising the model training and inference processes to ensure accurate diagnosis and treatment recommendations can be obtained promptly during clinical emergencies. This may involve optimising data transmission and processing speeds, designing efficient model architectures, and implementing real-time monitoring and feedback mechanisms to enable timely decision-making in urgent situations. Regarding cross-institutional collaboration, while ensuring compliance with patient data regulations, FL platforms need to strictly adhere to data privacy regulations and medical ethical requirements to ensure the compliance and confidentiality of patient data. Furthermore, the platform should provide secure data-sharing mechanisms among medical institutions and ensure secure information transmission during cross-institutional collaboration through the integration of technological means and legal provisions.

To reduce the disparities in healthcare resources and diagnostic and treatment capabilities across different regions, FL platforms can implement intelligent scheduling and allocation mechanisms. These systems optimise the distribution of model training and data sharing according to the specific needs and resource availability of each region. Additionally, the platform can facilitate the sharing and collaboration of medical expertise among regions to improve the overall level of diagnosis and treatment. To ensure the standardisation and regularisation of platform services, future research can develop standardised guidelines applicable to FL platforms, covering aspects such as data sharing, privacy protection, and model evaluation. These standards can provide clear guidance for platform providers and participating institutions to ensure the robustness and credibility of the platform. Lastly, to enhance the scalability and personalisation of platform applications for AIS tasks, future research can explore customised models and algorithms tailored to specific AIS tasks to meet the needs of different medical institutions and clinical scenarios. Furthermore, the platform should offer flexible interfaces and customizable options, allowing institutions to tailor and optimise services according to their specific needs, thereby enabling personalised applications and services.

From a translational and technological standpoint, the integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) and diffusion models into CAI frameworks presents promising opportunities for advancing medical data generation and augmentation. By synthesizing de-identified clinical text and multi-modal imaging data, these models can enrich training datasets for AIS while safeguarding patient privacy. LLMs can generate structured reports and domain-specific knowledge representations to support model interpretability and human-AI collaboration, whereas diffusion models can produce realistic and diverse medical images to alleviate data scarcity and class imbalance across institutions. When combined with FL, such generative models enable privacy-preserving training and cross-institutional sharing of synthetic data, enhancing both scalability and fairness. Future research should focus on establishing rigorous validation protocols to ensure the clinical validity, bias control, and traceability of generated data, thereby enabling trustworthy and ethically compliant deployment of generative intelligence in collaborative healthcare ecosystems.

The application of CAI in AIS diagnosis and treatment holds great potential to transform the management of this critical condition. By enabling collaboration across multiple institutions, FL facilitates the development of robust and accurate models that enhance diagnostic precision while ensuring patient data privacy and security. FL platforms, such as FedEYE, can be customised to address the unique challenges of AIS, providing tailored solutions that consider the heterogeneous nature of patient populations, varying institutional needs, and the integration of multimodal data.

As FL platforms evolve, ongoing research and innovation in FL methodologies will be crucial to refining their applications in AIS and ensuring their effectiveness. Additionally, standardised guidelines and regulatory frameworks will be essential to guide the ethical and responsible implementation of FL in clinical settings. The scalability and flexibility of FL also allow smaller healthcare institutions with limited resources to participate in collaborative learning, gaining access to expert-level models and improving diagnostic capabilities without heavy computational infrastructure. Ultimately, FL’s ability to foster cross-institutional collaboration, safeguard patient privacy, and adapt to the needs of diverse healthcare institutions makes it a transformative technology poised to shape the future of AIS diagnosis and treatment.
